x: Baking soda, NaHCO₃, releases CO₂ in baking and neutralises stomach acid. Na₂CO₃ is washing soda and Mg(OH)₂ is Milk of Magnesia, also an antacid but not used in baking.
t: Check that the chemical fits both uses.

x: 2,4-D is a selective herbicide that kills broadleaf weeds. Allethrin is a mosquito repellent, Bordeaux mixture a fungicide and zinc phosphide a rat poison.
t: Classify each pesticide by its target.

x: Pyrex is borosilicate glass, which resists heat shock, so it is used for lab glassware. Soda-lime glass is for bottles and Crookes glass for sunglasses.
t: Recall the use of each type of glass.

x: Option B is incorrect: DDT is non-biodegradable and persists, building up in food chains. SO₂, N₂O and CFCs are correctly linked to their effects.
t: Recall DDT as a persistent pollutant.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Freon is a CFC, and CFCs release chlorine in the stratosphere that destroys ozone.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Lead-acid is the conventional battery, Ni-Cd a rechargeable battery, selenium a photoconductor and lithium compounds go into Li-ion cells, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the use of each material.

x: Silver iodide and dry ice seed clouds, sodium benzoate preserves soft drinks and zinc phosphide kills rats, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the use of each chemical.

x: All four are correct: CO₂ is the most common gas extinguisher, the soda-acid type makes CO₂ from NaHCO₃ and H₂SO₄, and CCl₄ was an older liquid type.
t: Recall the types of fire extinguisher.

x: Both are true: silicon is used in chips, solar cells and transistors, and germanium was used in early transistors.
t: Recall the semiconductors.

x: Two are insecticides: DDT and BHC. 2,4-D is a herbicide and zinc phosphide a rodenticide.
t: Classify each pesticide by its target.

x: Baking soda is keyed as the cleaning chemical, being a mild abrasive and deodoriser. Washing soda and ammonia also clean, so the question is loose.
t: Recall the household uses of baking soda.

x: Both are true: washing soda is Na₂CO₃ and is used for washing and to soften hard water.
t: Recall the uses of washing soda.

x: Bleaching powder releases chlorine, so it purifies water and bleaches. Cooking and preservation describe vinegar, and photography fixing describes hypo.
t: Recall the uses of bleaching powder.

x: Vinegar is dilute acetic acid, CH₃COOH, used in cooking and as a preservative. Na₂CO₃ is washing soda, NH₃ ammonia and Mg(OH)₂ milk of magnesia.
t: Recall the formula and use of vinegar.

x: Ammonia (NH₃) cleans glass, milk of magnesia (Mg(OH)₂) is an antacid, sodium benzoate preserves soft drinks and hypo (Na₂S₂O₃) fixes photographs, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the formula and use of each chemical.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the formula H₂SO₄ only identifies the acid; its strong acidity and dehydrating power explain its uses.
t: Check whether R explains the uses or only names the compound.

x: Nickel powder catalyses oil hydrogenation, which makes vanaspati, cryolite and bauxite are used to extract aluminium and silicon makes semiconductors, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the industrial use of each material.

x: Silicon makes chips, nichrome heating elements, zinc galvanises iron, and CuSO₄ (blue vitriol) is a fungicide and used in electroplating, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the use of each material.

x: Both are true: Freon was a common refrigerant, and CO₂ is used in fire extinguishers and fizzy drinks.
t: Recall the uses of Freon and CO₂.

x: All three are correct: silver bromide coats photographic plates, silver iodide seeds clouds and zinc phosphide is a rat poison.
t: Recall the uses of silver salts.

x: Bordeaux mixture is a fungicide, 2,4-D a herbicide, and allethrin and prallethrin are mosquito repellents, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Classify each pesticide by its target.

x: Both are true: Teflon is PTFE, used as a non-stick coating, and hypo is used in photography and as an antichlor.
t: Recall the uses of Teflon and hypo.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: SF₆ insulates electrical equipment, but its greenhouse strength comes from absorbing infrared and lasting thousands of years.
t: Check whether R is a cause or a separate use.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the sulphuric and nitric acids in acid rain react with the calcium carbonate of marble, eating away the Taj Mahal's surface.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: heavy water in high amounts is toxic and slows growth because deuterium alters the rate of biological reactions.
t: Recall the effects of heavy water.

x: I and II are correct: N₂O is laughing gas and is used as an anaesthetic. III is false because chlorine, not N₂O, disinfects water.
t: Recall the uses of nitrous oxide.

x: Both are true: formaldehyde and formic acid kill bacteria, but their use as food preservatives is limited.
t: Recall the antibacterial chemicals.

x: All four are correct: chlorine disinfects water by killing microbes, and chlorine-based tear gas irritates the eyes and airways.
t: Recall the uses of chlorine.

x: Selenium is photoconductive: its conductivity rises in light, so it is used in light sensors and photocopiers.
t: Recall the photoconductive material.

x: All four are keyed correct: hydrofluoric acid etches glass, diamond cuts glass, and silicon dioxide is the main part of ordinary glass.
t: Recall the chemistry of glass working.

x: The match tip has potassium chlorate, sulphur, starch and glue, the striking strip has red phosphorus and powdered glass, antimony trisulphide is the tip's fuel and SO₂ was an old refrigerant, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the chemistry of safety matches.

x: Liquid ammonia cools large cold stores, SO₂ was an early refrigerant, Freon was used in home refrigerators and N₂O is a greenhouse gas, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the history of refrigerants.

x: BHC stands for benzene hexachloride, C₆H₆Cl₆, an insecticide like lindane.
t: Recall the expansion of BHC.

x: All five are correct: allethrin, prallethrin, Sevin and Bt are insecticides used against mosquitoes and crop pests.
t: Recall the insecticides.

x: All four are correct: chloropicrin is a broad-spectrum fungicide, herbicide, insecticide and also a tear gas.
t: Recall the uses of chloropicrin.

x: All six are correct: sodium benzoate is E211, sorbates stop yeast and mould, SO₂ preserves dried fruit and wine, formic acid has limited use and propionates protect grains and cheese.
t: Recall the use of each preservative.

x: Both are true and R explains A: enzymes are called biocatalysts because they speed up the chemical reactions of living cells.
t: Check whether R defines A.

x: Platinum and rhodium are used in catalytic converters, nickel catalysts drive steam reforming of methane and steam reforming produces hydrogen, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
t: Recall the use of each catalyst.

x: Both are true: indium tin oxide is a transparent conductor used in smart films and conductive glass such as touch screens.
t: Recall the uses of ITO.

x: Two are fullerene and nanotube uses: lubricants and catalysts. Smart films and conductive glass use indium tin oxide.
t: Discriminate nano-carbon uses from ITO uses.

x: Both are true: fullerenes and nanotubes are research materials, and quantum dots are tiny semiconductor crystals.
t: Recall the nanomaterials.

x: Nano-fabrication of silicon is central to advanced semiconductor research and chip making. ITO is for displays and selenium for sensors.
t: Recall the nano uses of silicon.

x: Both are true and R is keyed as explaining A: burning plastics and PET is how they pollute, releasing CO₂ and other greenhouse gases.
t: Check whether R is the process behind A.

x: Mercury was used in thermometers because it expands evenly and stays liquid over a wide range. Silver salts serve photography and cloud seeding.
t: Recall the uses of mercury.

x: Mercury thermometers are now restricted because mercury is toxic; digital thermometers have largely replaced them.
t: Recall the current status of mercury devices.

x: Soda-lime glass makes bottles and windows, Crookes glass makes UV-blocking sunglasses using cerium, and cobalt oxide colours glass deep blue, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the types and colourings of glass.

x: Both are true: CCl₄ is carbon tetrachloride, and Pyrene was the old CCl₄ liquid extinguisher.
t: Recall the old fire extinguishers.

x: All three are correct: Bordeaux mixture is copper sulphate with lime, and fungicides protect crops and are used in water tanks.
t: Recall the make-up of Bordeaux mixture.

x: Both are true: vinegar (acetic acid) is used to preserve and flavour pickles and sauces.
t: Recall the uses of vinegar.

x: Silicon's symbol is Si and germanium's Ge, giving a-i, b-ii. NH₃ and Na₂CO₃ are distractors.
t: Recall element symbols.

x: Diamond is the hardest natural substance, 10 on the Mohs scale. Talc is the softest mineral and tungsten is a hard metal, not the hardest substance.
t: Recall the hardness extremes.

x: Option C is incorrect: oxygen is about 21% of the air; 78% is nitrogen. Hydrogen is about 75% of the universe, and oxygen is the most abundant element in the crust.
t: Discriminate nitrogen (78%) from oxygen (21%).

x: Both are true and R explains A: hydrogen's atomic weight of about 1.008 is the smallest of any element, which is why it is the lightest.
t: Check whether R is the reason for A.

x: Diamond is 10 on the Mohs scale, talc is used in baby powder, lithium has density 0.534 g/cm³ and osmium 22.61 g/cm³, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the record properties of each substance.

x: All three are correct: hydrogen is about 75% of the universe, oxygen 46.6% of the crust, and aluminium is the third most abundant crustal element.
t: Recall the abundance order in the crust: O, Si, Al, Fe.

x: Both are true: hydrogen burns only to water, and ammonia dissolves readily because it is polar and hydrogen-bonds with water.
t: Recall why hydrogen is clean and ammonia is soluble.

x: Two are strong bases: NaOH and KOH. Mg(OH)₂ and Al(OH)₃ are weak bases used in antacids.
t: Discriminate strong alkalis from weak antacid bases.

x: Tungsten boils at about 5555°C, far above acetic acid, hydrogen peroxide and ethanol, which boil near or below 150°C.
t: Recall tungsten's record boiling and melting points.

x: Tungsten is listed as the hardest metal. Gold and platinum are soft, and osmium is the densest metal.
t: Discriminate hardest (tungsten) from densest (osmium).

x: Talc is hydrated magnesium silicate, Mg₃Si₄O₁₀(OH)₂. Mg(OH)₂ is milk of magnesia and Al(OH)₃ an antacid.
t: Recall the formula of talc.

x: Both are true: sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife, and both are alkali metals of Group 1.
t: Recall the properties of alkali metals.

x: Lithium is 0.534 g/cm³, potassium 0.86, sodium 0.97 and osmium 22.61, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the densities of alkali metals and osmium.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Li, Na and K are less dense than water (below 1 g/cm³), so they float.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All four are correct: osmium is the densest metal, and uranium (Z = 92, density 19.05 g/cm³) is the heaviest naturally occurring element.
t: Discriminate densest metal from heaviest natural element.

x: All four are correct: platinum (21.09 g/cm³) is denser than gold (19.3), which is denser than mercury (13.6).
t: Recall the densities of heavy metals.

x: Both are true and R explains A: potassium tops the reactivity series because it loses its single outer electron most easily.
t: Check whether R is the basis of A.

x: Both are true: fluorine is the most reactive non-metal and halogen, and it has the highest electronegativity (4.0).
t: Recall fluorine's record properties.

x: The key gives the series as printed, K > Na > Ca > Hg > Ag > Au > Mg…, which misplaces the noble metals. The true order is K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au, so no option is correct.
t: Recall the true reactivity series and check where the noble metals sit.

x: All three are correct: gold is the least reactive metal, occurs native, and with platinum and silver is a noble metal.
t: Recall the noble metals.

x: All five are correct: helium is second in cosmic abundance, silicon and aluminium are 27.7% and 8.1% of the crust, and argon and CO₂ are 0.93% and about 0.03% of the air.
t: Recall the abundance figures.

x: Both are true and R explains A: about 60% of the body is water, and oxygen makes up most of its mass, so oxygen is the most abundant element.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Cellulose, the main material of plant cell walls, is the most abundant organic compound on Earth. Silicon is an element, not an organic compound.
t: Recall the most abundant organic compound.

x: All four are correct: boron melts at 2453 K, iron 1808 K, silicon 1693 K and aluminium 933 K, giving B > Fe > Si > Al.
t: Recall the melting-point order.

x: All four are correct: tungsten melts near 3422°C, which suits filaments, tin–lead solder melts near 183°C, and Teflon near 327°C.
t: Recall the melting points of materials.

x: Both are true: liquid hydrogen boils at −252.9°C, so it must be stored as a cryogenic liquid.
t: Recall the boiling point of hydrogen.

x: Three are correct: gold is about 19.3 g/cm³, mercury 13.6 and steel 7.8. Statement 4 gives mercury's density for gold.
t: Check each density figure against its metal.

x: Lithium, at 0.534 g/cm³, is the lightest metal and floats on water. Aluminium is light but much denser at 2.7.
t: Recall lithium as the lightest metal.

x: Silver is the best electrical conductor, mercury the best heat conductor among the liquids, selenium a photoconductor and mica a heat conductor that insulates electrically, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the conduction record holders.

x: Both are true: silver conducts heat best, and sulphur, phosphorus and bromine are poor electrical conductors.
t: Recall the conduction properties of elements.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: complete ionisation is what defines a strong acid, not a separate reason why these three acids are strong.
t: Check whether R is a reason or a definition.

x: Aqua regia is 3 parts concentrated HCl to 1 part concentrated HNO₃. The other ratios reverse or change the mix.
t: Recall the 3:1 HCl to HNO₃ ratio.

x: Aqua regia dissolves the noble metals gold and platinum, which no single acid can attack.
t: Recall what aqua regia dissolves.

x: All three are correct: NaOH makes hard soap, KOH soft soap, and Mg(OH)₂ is milk of magnesia.
t: Recall the uses of common bases.

x: Both are true: water is a polar solvent with a high dipole moment, so it dissolves ionic salts best.
t: Recall why water is a good solvent.

x: Both are true: ionic compounds dissolve poorly in less polar alcohol, and hard water's Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ stop soap lathering.
t: Recall solubility and hard water.

x: All three are correct: mercury is the poorest heat conductor among metals at about 8.3 W/mK, and silver is the best conductor of both heat and electricity.
t: Recall the conduction extremes among metals.

x: Statement A is true: mercury conducts heat worse than lead. Statement B is false because it reverses that comparison.
t: Check for a reversed comparison.

x: Both are true and R explains A: gold, platinum and silver are noble, so they react so little that they occur free in nature.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.
